title: Gecko Feet Hold 290 Pounds. What If You Had Them? 🦎
description:
How do geckos stick to walls with no glue? Millions of tiny hairs on gecko toes use van der Waals forces, and here's what it would take for human feet to do the same.

Sources:

topic: What if humans had a gecko's sticky feet?
script:
What if your feet could hold 290 pounds with no glue?
A gecko's feet can, at least in theory.
Its toes are covered in tiny hairs,
about six and a half million on one gecko.
And every hair splits into hundreds of even tinier tips.
Those tips get so close to the wall
that the molecules themselves pull together.
It's called the van der Waals force.
One hair is weak,
but millions together are mighty.
To let go, a gecko just peels its toes up,
like tape.
Now scale that up to you.
You'd need sticky pads on forty percent of your body,
about eighty percent of your front!
And your shoes? US size one hundred fourteen.
That's why geckos are about the biggest animals that can do this.
So would you trade your feet for gecko feet?
key_facts: A gecko has about 6.5 million setae (hairs); together they could theoretically support about 130 kg / 290 lb (Autumn & Hansen, SICB)
Setae stick by van der Waals forces; each splits into many tiny spatula tips
A human would need adhesive pads on about 40% of body surface (~80% of the front), shoes EU 145 / US 114 (Labonte et al., PNAS 2016, Cambridge)
Geckos are about the largest animals that can climb smooth walls with sticky pads
